intro: Use “there is” and “there are” to say that something exists or is in a place. You need them to describe a town, a house, a fridge or a situation.
objectifs: Choose between there is (singular, uncountable) and there are (plural).
Make negatives (there isn't, there aren't, there's no) and questions (Is there…? Are there any…? How many… are there?).
Know the difference between there is and it is, and between there / their / they're.
Avoid word-for-word translations: for past time use ago; for distance use it's.

texte: Use “there is” (short form: there's) before a singular or uncountable noun, and “there are” before a plural noun. In writing, “there are” has no short form.
The verb agrees with the noun that follows. In a list, it usually agrees with the first thing: There's a table and four chairs. There are four chairs and a table.

lignes: there is / there's + a / an + noun
There's a bank near the station.
There's some milk in the fridge.
There are two bakeries in my street.
there are + a lot of / many / some + noun
There are a lot of tourists in summer.

exemples: There's a cat in the garden.
Singular.
There are thirty students in my class.
Plural.
There's a lot of traffic today.
Uncountable → is.

texte: Put “not” after is / are: there isn't (there is not), there aren't (there are not). Before a plural or uncountable noun, we often add “any”: There aren't any shops. There isn't any bread. (Some and any: lesson 31.)
Another very common way: “there's no” / “there are no” + noun, with no article: There's no bus today. There are no taxis. With “no”, the verb stays positive: never “there isn't no”.
exemples: There isn't a hospital in my village.
isn't + a.
There aren't any chairs in this room.
aren't + any.
There's no sugar in my coffee.
there's no + noun.

texte: For questions, change the order: Is there…? Are there…? With plural and uncountable nouns, we often add “any”. Short answers: Yes, there is. / No, there isn't. Yes, there are. / No, there aren't. Like with “to be”, no short form after Yes (not “Yes, there's”).
To ask about quantity: How many + plural noun + are there? / How much + uncountable noun + is there? (lesson 30).

lignes: Is there a pharmacy near here?

exemples: Excuse me, is there a cash machine near here?
A useful question in town.
How many people are there in your family?
How many + plural.

sections.titre: There is or it is? There, their or they're?
texte: “There is” introduces something for the first time (it exists). “It is” describes or identifies something we already know about. We often use them one after the other: There's a new café on my street. It's very nice.

Don't confuse “there are” and “they are” either: There are two parks in my town. They are big and green. And in writing: there (in that place), their (possessive), they're (= they are) sound the same (lesson 14).
exemples: There's a parcel for you. It's from Canada.
Introduce, then describe.
There are some new students. They're from Belgium.
there are, then they are.

sections.titre: When not to use there is
texte: For a time in the past, English uses “ago” after the period: two years ago (you will see it at A2 with the past simple). For distance, use “it's”: It's 5 km from here.
To describe a place, don't put the place as a subject with “has” in the wrong order: say “In my town, there's a cinema” or “My town has a cinema”, never “In my town has a cinema”.
To ask about a problem, say “What's wrong?” or “What's the matter?”, not “What is there?”.

lignes: I arrived, and now it is two days later
the distance to the beach is 10 km
you want to know the problem

formule: There's + singular / uncountable · There are + plural · Is there…? / Are there any…? · There isn't / aren't (any) · There's no…
prononciation: “There's” /ðeəz/ is one syllable. “there are” often joins: /ðeər ə/ (in British English, the r is pronounced before a vowel).
In the sentence, “there” is weak: /ðə/ (There's a cat /ðəz ə ˈkæt/). The noun has the stress.
Question (Is there a bank?): your voice goes up. “How many… are there?”: your voice goes down.
“isn't” /ˈɪznt/ and “aren't” /ɑːnt/: stress them so people hear the negative.
erreurs: There is two banks.
There are two banks.
Plural → there are.
There are a lot of traffic.
There's a lot of traffic.
Uncountable → there is.
In my town has a cinema.
In my town, there's a cinema. / My town has a cinema.
Use there is to say something exists.
There isn't no milk.
There's no milk. / There isn't any milk.
No double negative.
Is there a bank? — Yes, there's.
Yes, there is.
No short form in a positive short answer.
There is two years, I was in Paris.
Two years ago, I was in Paris.
Past time = period + ago.
It's a cat in the garden.
There's a cat in the garden.
To say something exists, use there is.

dialogue.contexte: A Belgian student who is new in Québec City visits a flat with the landlord.
lignes: So, this is the flat. There are two bedrooms and a small living room.
It's nice. Is there a washing machine?
No, there isn't, but there's a laundry room in the basement.
OK. And are there any shops near here?
Yes, there are. There's a supermarket on the corner and there are two cafés on the next street.
Great. How many people are there in the building?
There are six flats, so about ten people. It's very quiet.
Perfect. There's just one problem: there's no desk!
No problem. There's an old desk in my garage. You can have it.

mots: bedroom
There are three bedrooms in the house.
a room where you sleep
living room
There's a big sofa in the living room.
the room where you relax and watch TV
kitchen
Is there a microwave in the kitchen?
the room where you cook
bathroom
There's no bath in the bathroom, only a shower.
the room where you wash
fridge
There isn't any milk in the fridge.
a machine that keeps food cold
supermarket
There's a supermarket on the corner.
a big shop that sells food and other things
pharmacy
Is there a pharmacy near here?
a shop that sells medicine (UK also: chemist's)
park
There are two parks in my town.
a green public area with grass and trees
building
There are six flats in this building.
a structure with walls and a roof, like a house or an office
near
Is there a bus stop near here?
not far away

exercices.consigne: Write the sentence in the negative (two possible forms: isn't / aren't any, or no).
items: There's a cinema in my village.
There isn't a cinema in my village. / There's no cinema in my village.
There are some eggs in the fridge.
There aren't any eggs in the fridge. / There are no eggs in the fridge.
There's some bread on the table.
There isn't any bread on the table. / There's no bread on the table.

exercices.consigne: Write the question, then the short answer shown.
items: a lift / in the building? (yes)
Is there a lift in the building? — Yes, there is.
any good restaurants / here? (no)
Are there any good restaurants here? — No, there aren't.
How many / students / in your class? (22)
How many students are there in your class? — There are twenty-two.
any milk / in the fridge? (no)
Is there any milk in the fridge? — No, there isn't.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: There is three bedrooms.
There are three bedrooms.
In my street has a bakery.
In my street, there's a bakery. / There's a bakery in my street.
There aren't no taxis.
There aren't any taxis. / There are no taxis.
There's a new restaurant. There's very good.
There's a new restaurant. It's very good.
Are there a park near here?
Is there a park near here?

exercices.consigne: Write one sentence with there is / there are for each situation.
items: You want to say that something is wrong: a problem exists.
There's a problem.
The room has no chairs.
There aren't any chairs. / There are no chairs.
You ask a stranger about shops in the area.
Are there any shops near here?
The metro is full of people.
There are a lot of people on the metro.

exercices.consigne: Describe your neighbourhood or village in five sentences with there is / there are, positive and negative, and ask a visitor one question.
items: Example answer
In my neighbourhood there's a big market and there are three schools. There's a pharmacy near my house. There isn't a cinema, but there are two cafés. Is there a cinema in your town?

a_retenir: There's + singular or uncountable; there are + plural.
Negative: there isn't / aren't (any) or there's no / there are no + noun.
Question: Is there…? Are there any…? → Yes, there is. / No, there aren't. How many… are there?
There is introduces, it is describes: There's a café. It's nice.
Past time = period + ago; distance = it's.
